text: You now know how site-to-site VPN and ExpressRoute or Direct Connect each work. This lesson is about which one you'd actually choose for a given workload, because in practice it's rarely obvious -- and it's almost never a simple "dedicated is always better." Both answers are correct in the right circumstances, and a working architect has to be able to justify whichever one they pick.

Site-to-site VPN is fast to set up -- often a single afternoon -- and cheap, since it's purely a software and configuration task on both ends. ExpressRoute or Direct Connect takes real lead time, often weeks, because a connectivity provider has to physically provision a cross-connect at an exchange location, and it costs meaningfully more for the circuit and the port speed you commit to.

The decision comes down to the workload. Moderate, bursty traffic where latency variability is tolerable, and where fast setup matters more than peak performance, fits VPN well -- a nightly backup job doesn't care if one tunnel's round-trip time wobbles a little. Sustained high-bandwidth, latency-sensitive, or compliance-driven primary production traffic fits a dedicated circuit -- no amount of VPN tuning changes the fact the traffic still, technically, crosses the public internet underneath the encryption.

That compliance detail matters more than raw traffic volume. A rule that data must never transit the public internet at all can't be satisfied by any VPN, however strong its encryption -- only a dedicated circuit satisfies it, even for a workload moving a comparatively modest amount of data each day.

A common real pattern uses both: a dedicated circuit as the primary path for production traffic, with site-to-site VPN configured as automatic failover if the circuit goes down. That gets consistent day-to-day performance plus a cheap, fast-to-restore fallback, instead of zero connectivity while a physical circuit issue gets fixed. Next: point-to-site VPN, for a single remote user's laptop instead of a whole network.
